sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Name three things you can order in a café, then say one price aloud.
items: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee, bitte.
sections.lede: Say each line aloud once. This section is not scored.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: These are the three things you will be able to do by the end of the lesson.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Order politely, ask for the price and understand the bill.

blocks.text: The most useful café phrase at A1 is "Ich hätte gern …", which means "I would like …". It is softer than "Ich will" and works in cafés, shops and restaurants. The item after it is in the accusative: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.

To ask for the price, use "Was kostet …?" for one item or "Was kosten …?" for several. The answer often comes as a number plus Euro: "Das macht drei Euro fünfzig." For the bill, ask "Die Rechnung, bitte."

blocks.title: Polite without being complicated
blocks.text: Learn "Ich hätte gern …" as one fixed phrase. You do not need to conjugate hätte again in the same sentence.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

rows: Ask for the bill at the end of a meal.

items: Use einen for masculine items in the accusative: einen Kaffee, einen Tee.
Use eine for feminine items: eine Limonade, eine Suppe.
Use ein for neuter items: ein Wasser, ein Brot.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short, focused sound work. Play each item and repeat it twice.

items.hint: Stress the second syllable: ka-FEE, with a long e.
The ch after n is soft; the final -ung is a clear oong.
The ä is short and open, like the e in "bet".

blocks.text: In many German cafés you order at the table and pay at the end. It is normal to ask for the bill when you are ready, rather than waiting for it to be brought automatically.
Card payments are common in cities, but some small bakeries and cafés still prefer cash. Asking "Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?" before you order is always acceptable.

sections.title: Dialogue in context
sections.lede: Read the scene, then play it and follow the speakers.
sections.setting: At a small café in Munich, Sara orders breakfast.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.de: Guten Morgen. Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und ein Brot.
lines.en: Good morning. I would like a coffee and a bread.

lines.speaker: Kellner
lines.de: Gern. Möchten Sie auch etwas Wasser?
lines.en: Certainly. Would you like some water too?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.en: Yes, please. How much is that?

lines.speaker: Kellner
lines.en: That comes to five euros twenty.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Ordering with hätte gern
sections.lede: The phrase is fixed, but the article after it follows the noun.

blocks.text: Use "Ich hätte gern …" for a polite order. "Ich möchte …" is also correct, but hätte gern is especially common in cafés.

sections.tip: Prices use a comma in German writing: 3,50 €. Say "drei Euro fünfzig".

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Order a drink and a snack, then ask for the price. Use hätte gern and Was kostet …?

model.de: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und ein Brot. Was kostet das?
model.en: I would like a coffee and a bread. How much is that?

tips: Use einen for masculine drinks such as Kaffee and Tee.
Add "bitte" to sound polite without changing the grammar.
Say the price back to practise the numbers: drei Euro fünfzig.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These are the errors learners most often make with this pattern.

items.why: Kaffee is masculine and the direct object, so ein becomes einen.
Brötchen is plural, so the verb must be kosten.
Ich will sounds blunt in a café; hätte gern is the polite standard.
